trimmingSuggestions.description: The lengthy interview with Dr. Mokgethi in Scenes 2, 4, and 5 could be trimmed to retain the most relevant information and explanations. Removing repetitive statements and focusing on key points would increase the dynamism of the video.

text_to_speech: Cancer patients in Gauteng often die while waiting months for urgent treatment. The Cancer Alliance of South Africa has described this as a humanitarian crisis. I acknowledge that yes, we do have a crisis but we are also working to make sure that we address that. When Charlotte (Maxeke Hospital) was still operating normally, we did have a challenge but it was manageable. But then the fire happened at Charlotte (Maxeke). Then the pandemic happened, COVID happened. In the process of COVID we also lost a number of staff. So we are looking into filling those vacancies and also into making sure that we are revising our organisational structure so that we can have enough staff who can deal with the cancer patients. In April last year a fire engulfed parts of Charlotte Maxeke Hospital in Johannesburg, placing an enormous burden on already overcrowded public hospitals in surrounding areas. The reopening of the hospital's emergency unit has been postponed several times due to broken CT scan machines. That is what is delaying us to open the accident and emergency unit. But as for everything else, it's in place. The mental health ward that we identified there to use to offload pressure from Helen Joseph (Hospital), that is in place. So the only thing that is holding us back, because if you can get a trauma patient, then it means that you must send a patient to another hospital for a scan and then it's going to inconvenience us. MEC Mokgethi says the high influx of foreign nationals, especially for maternity care, is crippling the system. The challenge is that some of these women, when they come from their countries they never attended antenatal clinic, they come as emergencies. They are putting pressure on the system. The infrastructure of the hospital can only accommodate a certain number. MEC Mokgethi admits that the province's hospital infrastructure is crumbling. Since 1994 we only built one hospital in Gauteng which is Bheki Mlangeni and it is already also overflowing with patients. Most of our facilities, the aging infrastructure is so bad. So it is also a challenge for us to say we are operating with the facilities that were built years and years back with no anticipation of the increased disease burden that we are currently having, no anticipation of the increased population that we are currently having. While MEC Mokgethi admits that certain areas in our public health care system are buckling under immense pressure, she stopped short of calling it a crisis. I don't think to say it is a crisis, because there's a difference between pressure and a crisis. Because there are those areas of healthcare where there is an immense pressure, but there are those where we are doing very good. I think we can say there are challenges. We have a shortage of staff and we can attract and retain, especially the staff to take care of our cancer patients.
